Observed rates as draws

Source: R/derive-observed.R
mt_observed.Rd

Turns observed deaths and exposures into an mt_draws object whose paths are Poisson draws of the death counts given the exposures. All functions for draws then also describe the past, with intervals for the observed rates: life_expectancy(), asr(), prob_dying(), mt_contrast(), mt_inequality(). The derived quantities accept an mt_data object directly and call mt_observed() with its defaults.

Usage

mt_observed(data, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)

Arguments

data

An mt_data object with deaths and exposures on the grid.

n_draws

Number of draws.

seed

Random seed (default 1, so that results are reproducible).

Value

An mt_draws object with the observed periods (element observed: the observed rates; exposure: the exposures).

Details

The draws are a parametric bootstrap: Poisson counts with the observed deaths as their means, divided by the exposures (treated as known). The intervals of derived quantities therefore describe the Poisson variation of the counts around the observed values. A cell without deaths has mean zero and gets no variation, and the observed counts stand in for their unknown expected values, so intervals for small populations, with many cells of few or no deaths, are too narrow.

With n_draws = 1, the one draw holds the observed rates (for point values, as in mt_decompose()). Otherwise every draw is a Poisson draw, and the observed rates are kept in the element observed: the observed value is not one of the draws, so that means and quantiles describe the bootstrap distribution alone.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 2015:2019)
life_expectancy(x, at = 65)
